newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: More gloom seen for S.African shares next week.
newsitem.headline: More gloom seen for S.African shares next week.

text.p: Bashed by slides on Wall Street, manipulated by futures activity and weighed by renewed rand weakness, South African industrial shares are set to enter next week in gloom, local portfolio asset managers said Friday.

Facing the last full week of trade before the Christmas holidays, which contains a market holiday on Monday and the December equity futures close-out on Tuesday, trade is likely to be light but volatile in a market weakened by this week's damage.
"It's under pressure now. Generally it's going to be a very quiet week and I do think it will tend to drift down," said Raymond Goss, a portfolio manager at Irish & Co.

"It's going to be volatile because of Wall Street, the rand and also large basket trades which are not shy in affecting the prices. Things will be under pressure," said a senior portfolio asset manager who asked not to be identified.

Fooling world markets it had shrugged off negative interpretations of Federal Reserve Bank governor Alan Greenspan's recent comments, Wall Street seemed to hold its own at the week's start and world bourses breathed sighs of relief.
But then it fell and took South African stocks with it, sending them on a negative run which looks set to continue.

"The sentiment right now is obviously very negative and then you add to that the rand, which is pretty weak. What dominates at the moment is concern about foreign stock markets, which are not looking good, thanks to Greenspan and a few other things as well," said an asset manager who asked not to be identified.

Some commentators said that the latest developments on Wall Street were not really spawned by panic and that players were simply hearing Greenspan's words, which implied U.S. markets were overheated, and re-evaluating their positions.

But for South African stocks, battered by economic and political anxiety the mere hint that all is not well on Wall Street has sent them reeling. November CPI inflation next week will also be the only local economic indicator offering direction.
By 1310 GMT on Friday the industrial index had lost 1.72 percent of its value, falling to 7,680.2 points. The all-share index was cut by 1.92 percent to 6,480.3 points.

Even record volumes are no promise of paradise as the more than one billion rand turnover on Thursday included a large asset swap which commentators say saw South African stocks flow back in, indicating waning foreign confidence in the market.
"Yesterday's big equity transactions was in fact stock that actually came back from overseas, flowing back into South Africa which is not a good sign at all," one dealer said.
Large volumes were seen for the futures close-out on Tuesday but after that trade was expected to quieten down ahead of the festive season holidays.
"We can expect some good volumes on the close-out, but on the week it will be a little bit lower," Goss said.

While the overall trend next week was expected to be down, commentators added that some respite could come from a quiet gilts market, with many traders already having closed their books, and also from futures players trying to pump up stocks ahead of close-out.

"Rumours are in the market that the guys will try to buy up those Industrial 25 stocks and will try to close slightly better on the Tuesday, but that is out of line with what the market is doing at the moment which is drifting," Goss said.
No major company results are due next week.
